haiku-low.q1: MySQL commits first, with a pending row in the same transaction. Then the copy to Postgres runs under the id lock. If Postgres fails, the caller still gets success.
haiku-low.q2: Only when the incoming row is missing from Postgres (insert), or the existing row's version is lower than the incoming one. Never when the id has a tombstone.
haiku-low.q3: Every app instance must be dual-writing (mysql_primary) and show it for at least 30 seconds. Instances can disagree for up to 30 seconds after a flag change.
haiku-low.q4: The backfill reads only the MySQL replica, in primary-key order, 2,000 rows per batch. It pauses while replica lag is above 5 seconds, rechecking every 5 seconds.
haiku-low.q5: Reads: a full comparison must find zero mismatches, then the ramp runs 1, 10, 50, 100 percent. Source of truth: reads at 100% on Postgres for at least 3 days, plus a clean comparer pass.
haiku-low.q6: The pending row, with a change_id, is stored in the source's database and committed with the write. The sweeper retries the copy until it lands; the comparer is a backstop.
haiku-low.q7: Every copy and every backfill batch row holds the per-user-id Postgres advisory lock, so copies never interleave. Every copy also checks the tombstone table and never writes an erased id.
haiku-low.q8: Progress is in backfill_progress.last_id in Postgres, committed in the same transaction as each batch. After a crash it restarts after last_id; it stops at the last id.
haiku-low.q9: The comparer walks both tables in primary-key order. Differences still present after a 5-minute re-read are repaired by copying; a target version higher than the source is not overwritten and is reported as a bug.
haiku-low.q10: Instances on the old mode keep writing until they see paused, and paused returns 503, so no mixing. If steps 2-3 exceed 45 seconds, the operator sets the old mode back.
haiku-low.q11: After the switch, Postgres assigns ids from its sequence, set above MySQL's AUTO_INCREMENT and the largest Postgres id. Rollback raises MySQL's AUTO_INCREMENT above the Postgres sequence and every tombstoned id.
haiku-low.q12: Postgres-primary copies every write to MySQL with pending rows for 14 days. Rollback runs the switch procedure to mysql_primary, then sets read_from_pg to 0. The option ends at step 10, postgres_only.

sonnet.q1: MySQL is written first (one transaction that changes the row and writes a pending row with a new change_id), then the row is copied to Postgres. If the Postgres part fails or times out, the caller still gets success; the pending row stays and the sweeper copies it later.
sonnet.q2: Only if the row is missing (insert), or the existing Postgres row's version is lower than the incoming version (replace). Also never if a tombstone exists for that id. Nothing else.
sonnet.q3: Every app instance must be dual-writing (users.write_mode = mysql_primary, shown on app_flag_value for at least 30 seconds) before backfill starts. Instances can disagree for up to 30 seconds after a flag change (flags refresh every 30 seconds).
sonnet.q4: It reads only the MySQL replica (not the primary), in primary-key order, 2,000 rows per batch, and checks replica lag before each batch; if lag (mysql_replica_lag_seconds) is above 5 seconds it waits, rechecking every 5 seconds. The replica is shared with reporting jobs.
sonnet.q5: Reads move to Postgres only after a full comparison (comparer pass) finds zero confirmed mismatches. The source of truth moves only after reads have been 100% on Postgres for at least 3 days (and the last comparer pass was clean).
sonnet.q6: The pending row (user id plus change_id) records it. It is kept in the source database's pending table, i.e. MySQL's pending table in mysql_primary mode (written in the same transaction as the change). The sweeper (timer every 30 seconds on workers, no Redis) retries the copy and deletes the pending row once the copy succeeds and the change_id is unchanged.
sonnet.q7: Tombstones: erasure writes a row in user_tombstones holding the id, and every copy (backfill, repair, sweeper, dual write) checks it and never writes that id. Copies also hold the per-user-id Postgres advisory lock so inserts, erasures and tombstone checks do not interleave.
sonnet.q8: In the backfill_progress table in Postgres (last_id). Each batch is one Postgres transaction that copies the rows and sets last_id to the batch's last id, committed together, so progress matches copied rows. It stops when it reaches the last id (the end of the table in primary-key order); then the comparer runs.
sonnet.q9: The comparer. It walks both tables in primary-key order, 2,000 rows per page, comparing presence, version, every column and tombstone status. A difference counts only if it persists when re-read from the source primary 5 minutes later; confirmed mismatches are repaired with the copy rules. If the target version is higher than the source, it is not overwritten and is reported as a bug.
sonnet.q10: A manual switch procedure: set write_mode to paused; wait until app_flag_value shows all instances paused (up to 30 seconds), writes get a retryable 503 once paused; wait 5 seconds and confirm the old source's pending table is empty; set the new id counter; then set the new mode and wait until all instances show it (restart any that don't). If steps 2-3 are not done within 45 seconds, the operator sets the old mode back and instances resume on the old mode with no write lost. Total pause per instance is at most about 75 seconds (target max 90).
sonnet.q11: Postgres assigns ids from its sequence. Collisions are avoided by setting the counter at switch step 4: planned switch sets the Postgres sequence to the larger of MySQL's AUTO_INCREMENT and the largest Postgres id plus 1. On rollback, MySQL's AUTO_INCREMENT is raised to the larger of its own value and the Postgres sequence's next value (needed for tombstone-only ids). Too-low counters cause duplicate-key errors, never overwrites.
sonnet.q12: In postgres_primary mode each write commits to Postgres then is copied to MySQL (pending rows in Postgres, sweeper retries), and the comparer keeps checking. Rollback: run the switch procedure with mysql_primary as the new mode, then set users.read_from_pg to 0. The option ends when the first instance runs postgres_only, which is done no sooner than 14 days after Postgres became the source (and with Postgres pending table empty); the MySQL table is dropped only after that. Switching to Postgres again restarts the 14 days.
